§6.2 Line Breaks Inside a Block

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

text-line-breaks-inside-a-block · text layout line-breaks

✅ Normative

One printed block set on several lines MUST stay one element, with a plain newline between its printed lines — no trailing spaces, no <br>. The same spelling MUST be used for every multi-line block in the document. Inside a table cell, where a newline cannot be written, the break is <br>.

One printed block that runs to more than one line because the page sets it that way: a stacked masthead, a postal address, a two-line banner, a title broken across a rule. The lines belong together; only the typesetting separates them.

MEREVALD                     ← one block, two printed lines
Merevald Retail Ltd

Settled: the block stays whole

  • One printed block MUST be one element, whatever break is written between its lines. Two stacked lines of a masthead MUST NOT become two headings, two paragraphs, or a heading with a subtitle. Splitting it is the never invent failure: the page printed one block, and a split claims it printed two.
  • Whether lines form one block is judged by the printing, not the wording: a single set, a single alignment and a single leading mean one block, even when the two lines read as separable phrases.

The break is a plain newline

The Markdown source keeps every printed line on its own source line. A renderer shows a single newline inside a paragraph as a space, so a rendered view runs the lines together; that is a display artefact, not a change to the output, which is judged on its source (see Numbered Section Headings§6.5 for the same principle). Two trailing spaces are invisible and are stripped by most whitespace normalisation; <br> puts markup on every line. Neither is used outside table cells.

  • The break MUST be a plain newline, and the same spelling MUST be used for every multi-line block in the document — paragraphs, addresses, headers and footers alike.
  • Inside a table cell a newline cannot be written, so a printed break there is <br> — see Record Groups and Multi-Line Cells§9.5.3.
  • A line that Markdown would parse as a list item or heading (- , 1. , # at its start) is escaped — see Escaping Printed Marks§7.2.4.

Not this rule's case

  • A rule printed between blocks is a separator, not a break inside one — see Line Separators and Breaks§6.3.
  • A line that wraps because it ran out of column width is not a printed break at all: its lines MUST be joined with a space.
  • Text whose line breaks carry meaning, such as verse, is governed by Verse and Hard Line Breaks§7.2.13.

Related

  • Line Separators and Breaks§6.3 — a rule between blocks, which resolves differently
  • Verse and Hard Line Breaks§7.2.13 — text whose breaks are content
